dish:Bouillabaisse.name: Bouillabaisse
dish:Bouillabaisse.text: The famous rockfish stew, born from fishermen's unsellable catch: rascasse (scorpionfish) is essential, and since the 1980 Marseille charter the ritual is fixed — the saffron-orange broth first, with rouille and croutons, then the fish on a platter after. Eaten all along the Var, but be honest about its passport. Origin Marseille (Bouches-du-Rhone) — not really a Var dish

dish:Soupe de poissons.name: Soupe de poissons
dish:Soupe de poissons.text: Bouillabaisse's humble, everyday cousin and what most Var bistros actually pour: rockfish simmered and then strained into a rust-coloured broth with no whole fish, served with rouille, garlic croutons and grated gruyere to raft on top. Origin Provencal coast, generally

dish:Cade toulonnaise.name: Cade toulonnaise
dish:Cade toulonnaise.text: Toulon's own chickpea-flour galette, baked thin in wide copper pans over a wood fire — a Ligurian cousin of Nice's socca. Legend has it Napoleonic soldiers brought it and 'caldo' (hot) became 'cade.' The true Toulon apero, and a star of the Sanary market. Origin Toulon

dish:Chichi fregi.name: Chichi fregi
dish:Chichi fregi.text: A sugared fried doughnut of wheat and chickpea flour, sold from seafront kiosks — with the cade, one of only two dishes claimed as 100% Toulonnais. Beach food, defended locally with near-religious fervour. Origin Toulon

dish:Daube provencale.name: Daube provencale
dish:Daube provencale.text: Beef simmered for hours in red wine with orange peel and herbs, traditionally in a bulbous clay or copper daubiere that rains the steam back over the meat. Peasant and carters' cooking; the name descends from Provencal 'adobar,' to prepare. Origin Provence (inland origins, carters between Haute-Provence and Aix/Marseille)

dish:Grand aioli.name: Grand aioli
dish:Grand aioli.text: Less a sauce than an occasion: a stiff, pungent emulsion of raw garlic, egg yolk and olive oil, whipped by hand and served with a mountain of poached salt cod, boiled vegetables, eggs and sea snails, dipped communally. A pillar of Provencal identity, usually a Friday feast. Origin Provence

dish:Pieds et paquets.name: Pieds et paquets
dish:Pieds et paquets.text: Sheep's trotters and little parcels of stuffed tripe stewed for most of a day in white wine and tomato — poverty cooking that wasted nothing, credited to Louis Ginouves around 1880. The Var eats it, but Marseille and Sisteron own it. Origin Marseille / Sisteron

dish:Tarte tropezienne.name: Tarte tropezienne
dish:Tarte tropezienne.text: A sugar-crusted brioche split and filled with two creams (pastry cream and buttercream), created in 1955 by Polish patissier Alexandre Micka in Saint-Tropez. Brigitte Bardot, filming 'And God Created Woman,' suggested the name; Micka trademarked it in 1973. Origin Saint-Tropez

dish:Tapenade.name: Tapenade
dish:Tapenade.text: The definitive rose-apero smear: black olives, capers (Provencal 'tapena,' hence the name) and anchovies pounded with olive oil. Invented in 1880 by chef Meynier at the restaurant La Maison Doree in Marseille — his original even carried tuna. Origin Marseille

dish:The tuna (thon).name: The tuna (thon)
dish:The tuna (thon).text: Mediterranean bluefin was once caught in madragues — vast net-mazes — off the Var coast from the 17th century; Brigitte Bardot's Saint-Tropez house, La Madrague, is named for one. The traps are all but gone now, but grilled tuna and thon a la provencale remain the coast's great fish. Origin Golfe de Saint-Tropez / Mediterranean tuna-trap heritage

st-tropez:Le Club 55.name: Le Club 55
st-tropez:Le Club 55.text: The founding legend of Pampelonne and the most famous beach club in the world. Bernard and Geneviève de Colmont built wooden cabins on the Ramatuelle sand in 1954; in 1955, seeing the family eating on the beach, a young Brigitte Bardot asked Geneviève to feed the crew of 'Et Dieu créa la femme.' The family's beach hut fed 80 people over the shoot — with no electricity, Geneviève borrowed a Saint-Tropez baker's oven to roast the beef — and 'Le Club 55' was born, named for the year. Their son Patrice de Colmont ran it from 1972 until his death in October 2025 at 77; his daughter Camille now runs it. The honest truth Not a party club — a lunch institution, and it trades hard on the legend. Book far ahead in season, expect Provençal classics at collector prices, and a paid sunbed on top; the scene is the point as much as the food. Signal Founded 1955 by Bernard and Geneviève de Colmont as the canteen for the Bardot film crew. Son Patrice ran it 1972–2025; now run by his daughter Camille, still family-owned and open.

st-tropez:Nikki Beach.name: Nikki Beach
st-tropez:Nikki Beach.text: The blueprint of the modern daytime-party beach club. The Miami brand chose Pampelonne for its second outpost, opening in summer 2002 with a grand-opening party still talked about on the strip. It set the template of DJ, pool, magnums and dancing-on-the-daybeds that much of Pampelonne now copies. The site was fully renovated in 2024, and from July 2026 its restaurant operates under a new name, Maurice à la Plage, while the venue itself stays open as Nikki Beach. The honest truth The champagne-spray, bottle-service archetype — loud, expensive and crowd-pleasing rather than discreet. Expect daybed minimums and a table spend that climbs fast once the music does. Signal Opened summer 2002 as the brand's first location outside Miami Beach; renovated 2024, restaurant rebranded 'Maurice à la Plage' for the 2026 season.

st-tropez:La Réserve à la Plage.name: La Réserve à la Plage
st-tropez:La Réserve à la Plage.text: The quiet-luxury answer to the party clubs, opened in 2019 as the beach arm of the five-star hotel La Réserve Ramatuelle. Owner Michel Reybier had Philippe Starck design a deliberately understated, bohemian-chic cabana, with a Mediterranean sharing menu overseen by Eric Canino, chef of the group's Michelin-starred restaurant La Voile. The honest truth Calm and design-led rather than a scene — which you pay handsomely for. This is a serious restaurant on the sand, priced accordingly, not a place to dance on the tables. Signal Opened 2019; Michel Reybier hotel group, interiors by Philippe Starck, cuisine under Eric Canino. Open for 2026 (roughly late April to early October).

st-tropez:Loulou / Moorea.name: Loulou / Moorea
st-tropez:Loulou / Moorea.text: Moorea is old Pampelonne — a beach that traces its roots back some seventy years to a bamboo straw hut with a barbecue and a few mattresses. Loulou, opened in 2019 by the Loulou Group, brought the glossy new-era 'art de vivre' concept to the same stretch, its name and 1950s-Riviera styling an homage to Loulou de la Falaise, Yves Saint Laurent's muse. The honest truth Loulou is firmly in the see-and-be-seen tier: designer crowd, high sunbed and dining minimums. The romance of Moorea's simple-hut origins is long gone from the prices. Signal Loulou opened 2019 (Loulou Group), named for YSL muse Loulou de la Falaise; Moorea one of Pampelonne's oldest beaches. Both open for 2026 (Loulou 23/04–03/10; Moorea 01/05–30/10).

st-tropez:Verde Beach.name: Verde Beach
st-tropez:Verde Beach.text: The music-forward, party-leaning option, on Pampelonne since 2019. It is run by the Paris-based Yeeels Group, founded by Alex Bril, and trades on driftwood-and-lounge daytime looks that tip into DJ-driven evenings. Regulars call it one of the more credible, music-first rooms on the strip. The honest truth Skews toward the party end — energetic and DJ-driven rather than restful. Expect a minimum spend and a crowd that comes to drink and dance, not to nap under a parasol. Signal Open since 2019; owned by the Yeeels Group (founder Alex Bril). Operating for the 2026 season.

st-tropez:Indie Beach.name: Indie Beach
st-tropez:Indie Beach.text: A free-spirited spot on the Pampelonne sand run by the Indie Group, built on the idea of a day that never quite ends — grilled fish and Mediterranean sharing plates at lunch, then DJ sets of indie, folk and electro that carry the crowd into the night under the stars. The honest truth The draw is the after-lunch-into-sunset drift rather than fine dining or exclusivity; a sunbed and drinks still add up to a proper Pampelonne bill. Signal Run by the Indie Group on Route de Bonne Terrasse, Ramatuelle; known for its evening DJ sets. Open for 2026 (roughly 28 April to 8 October).

st-tropez:Bagatelle.name: Bagatelle
st-tropez:Bagatelle.text: An import of a globe-trotting nightlife brand: after New York, Brazil and Saint-Barth, the Bagatelle owners brought their signature Mediterranean-food-plus-loud-music formula to Pampelonne. It runs the party-brunch template — chic décor, rosé, and a room that builds toward dancing. The honest truth The bottle-parade, magnum-and-sparklers school of beach dining; the food is secondary to the spectacle, and the bill reflects the show. A seasonal club, open roughly mid-April to mid-October. Signal A New York / Saint-Barth import brought to Pampelonne; open for the 2026 summer season (a daytime beach club, seasonal).

st-tropez:Les Caves du Roy.name: Les Caves du Roy
st-tropez:Les Caves du Roy.text: The legendary nightclub of Saint-Tropez, in the basement of the Hôtel Byblos. It opened in July 1967 — the Byblos was built by Lebanese businessman Jean-Prosper Gay-Para, the story goes, in tribute to Bardot — with a three-night launch stage-managed by Jacqueline Veyssière and guests including Juliette Gréco and Françoise Sagan. It has set the tone of Tropézien nights ever since. The honest truth The door is the whole experience, and it is famously selective. There is no real cover so much as an unspoken table minimum, and champagne is sold by the magnum at prices designed to thin the crowd. Signal Opened July 1967 in the Hôtel Byblos; running as the town's marquee club ever since. Open for 2026 (Byblos reopens 22 April; nightly from late June to late August).

st-tropez:Le VIP Room (now Lilly's Club).name: Le VIP Room (now Lilly's Club)
st-tropez:Le VIP Room (now Lilly's Club).text: The celebrity-magnet club built by Jean Roch, who cut his teeth on Saint-Tropez nightlife in 1989 running a back-room bar he named Hystéria before founding the VIP Room in 1997. Its guest list over the years ran to Jay-Z, Paris Hilton, Cara Delevingne and Jared Leto, with Dom Pérignon and surprise sets from big-name artists. After a farewell weekend on 3–5 April 2026, Jean Roch closed the VIP Room after 29 years; the same space now operates as Lilly's Club under new management. The honest truth No longer the VIP Room — the club closed for good in April 2026 and the room now runs as Lilly's Club, whose programme and scene are still taking shape. In its heyday, table service and bottle spend were effectively the price of entry, and the night lived and died by who was in the room. Signal Founded 1997 by Jean Roch (after his 1989 club Hystéria); closed after a final weekend 3–5 April 2026 and reborn as Lilly's Club.

st-tropez:Sénéquier.name: Sénéquier
st-tropez:Sénéquier.text: The red-awninged café-institution on the old port. The Sénéquier name dates to 1887, when Marie and Martin Sénéquier opened a pâtisserie (famous for a nougat recipe of the same year) at the Place aux Herbes; the business expanded to the quayside, where it became a café in 1930. Destroyed by bombardment in 1944 and rebuilt by 1951, its scarlet director's chairs and triangular tables are the town's front-row seat for watching the port — and everyone from fishermen to passing celebrities has taken one. The honest truth You pay tourist-port prices for a coffee, but the bill is really rent on the best people-watching terrace in Saint-Tropez. In August it is packed and priced to match. Signal A Sénéquier institution since 1887 (pâtisserie at Place aux Herbes); a quayside café since 1930, rebuilt after the war and reopened in 1951. Still trading.

gastronomy:Bandol.name: Bandol
gastronomy:Bandol.text: The Var's glory and the reason to take the region seriously. Mourvedre-led (minimum 50%), the reds are aged at least 18 months in large old oak foudres — tannic and closed young, built to run for decades. AOC since 1941. Domaine Tempier (the Peyraud family; farm since 1834) and Chateau de Pibarnon (vines on hand-built restanque terraces in a natural amphitheatre of blue marl) are the references. The rose is serious too — the one Provence pink genuinely worth cellaring a year.

gastronomy:Cotes de Provence.name: Cotes de Provence
gastronomy:Cotes de Provence.text: The workhorse and the volume: the largest Provencal appellation, roughly 20,000 hectares, about 90% of it rose (Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Rolle). Quality runs from industrial to genuinely fine. Its cooler inland sibling, Coteaux Varois en Provence around Brignoles, is often the better value.

gastronomy:Cassis.name: Cassis
gastronomy:Cassis.text: An honest edge case — just over the Var line in Bouches-du-Rhone, east of Marseille, entirely inside the Calanques National Park. One of France's first AOCs (1936) and, rare for Provence, a white-wine appellation (Marsanne, Clairette): saline and mineral, made for the sea urchins and grilled fish under the cliffs. Included because the terroir belongs to this coast even if the postcode doesn't.

gastronomy:Provence rose (the machine).name: Provence rose (the machine)
gastronomy:Provence rose (the machine).text: The caveat, told straight: Provence is the world's rose engine (about 40-45% of France's AOP rose, ~5% of global rose), and Sacha Lichine's Whispering Angel made pale pink a luxury category worth over a billion euros a year. Much of it is fashion, priced above reds of more substance. Drink it young, cold and local — but don't mistake the colour for the region's real depth, which is in Bandol.

coffee-scene:Cafés Magali.name: Cafés Magali
coffee-scene:Cafés Magali.label: Toulon (city centre
coffee-scene:Cafés Magali.hook: The real specialty anchor of the department. A house roaster running since 1928 that pivoted hard into café de spécialité when Frédéric De Barros took over in 2021 — lighter, single-origin, unburnt — and finally opened a proper tasting/coffee-shop counter in 2025. Order whatever the current filter lot is and let them talk you through it.

coffee-scene:Le Jardin du Café.name: Le Jardin du Café
coffee-scene:Le Jardin du Café.label: Hyères (old town
coffee-scene:Le Jardin du Café.hook: Half roastery, half fine-grocery, tucked in the medieval centre. Sylvain Daronian roasts roughly fifteen origins on-site and you come as much to be interrogated about your machine and your palate as to buy beans. Also 60-odd teas and Provençal oils/honey. A talking shop, not a brunch room.

coffee-scene:Lorgues Coffee Roasters (La.label: Lorgues
coffee-scene:Lorgues Coffee Roasters (La.hook: The one genuinely third-wave, Anglophone-style operation in the Var. Hamish and Veruschka Menlove, who came from Australia in 2017, roast 100% arabica single-origin lots and sell them from a barn-concept store. Worth the drive if you're already going inland — call ahead or check their current market schedule, as they've also sold at regional Provençal markets.

coffee-scene:Cafés Maurice.label: Toulon (Place Camille Ledeau
coffee-scene:Cafés Maurice.hook: Heritage more than third-wave, and honest about it: a family roasting name founded in 1875, dormant for generations, then revived in 2020 by a descendant. Everything is roasted in-house; drink it on a terrace in the pedestrian quarter or at the Sanary shop. Come for the revived craft and a decent cup, not a competition espresso.

coffee-scene:Torréfaction La Cigale.label: La Seyne-sur-Mer (downtown
coffee-scene:Torréfaction La Cigale.hook: A small weekly-batch roaster across the bay from Toulon — 100% arabica, each lot from a single terroir, roasted fresh, with a modest tea-salon corner. More a bean shop than a sit-down café, so treat it as a supply stop rather than a room to linger in.

natural-wine:Superbuvette.name: Superbuvette
natural-wine:Superbuvette.label: Toulon (Rue des Arts quarter
natural-wine:Superbuvette.hook: The clearest expression of living-wine culture in the Var: a vintage-furnished neighbourhood cave-bar pouring only natural and 'living' wines, plus a short vegetal plate — seasonal dips, a vinegar-marinated hard-boiled egg, local cheese and olives. Terrace, no pretension.

natural-wine:Les Quilles.name: Les Quilles
natural-wine:Les Quilles.label: Toulon (6 Place d'Armes)
natural-wine:Les Quilles.hook: A tiny 30 m² cave whose whole point is the person behind the counter and a tightly-chosen natural list that leans into local Var growers (carignan, grenache) and Bandol reds. The kind of place where you buy one bottle and leave with three recommendations; an adjoining bistro, Le Pas de Côté, sits alongside.

natural-wine:La Dégust' Nature.label: Toulon (48 Cours Lafayette

natural-wine:L'Épicerie Simple.label: Toulon

Opening days are limited (roughly Wed–Sat lunch, Fri–Sat dinner, Sunday brunch), so verify before making a special trip.

What Hyères does have are serious cavistes with an organic/biodynamic/natural bent (Cave de la Capte, on the Giens road; Vert d'Olive) for bottles to take away. Buy here, drink in Toulon.

listening:Villa Noailles.name: Villa Noailles
listening:Villa Noailles.label: Hyères (Montée de Noailles
listening:Villa Noailles.hook: The cultural gravity centre of the whole coast. Robert Mallet-Stevens' modernist villa (built 1923–33) for patrons Charles and Marie-Laure de Noailles — who bankrolled Cocteau, Man Ray, Buñuel — is now a national-interest art centre programming design, photography and fashion year-round, and hosting Design Parade each summer.

Treat it as a diggers' room, not a cocktail-and-vinyl bar.

around:Gorges du Verdon & Lac de Sainte-.label: ~1h45–2h drive north (full day trip)
around:Gorges du Verdon & Lac de Sainte-.hook: Europe's grandest limestone canyon, dropping to nearly 700 m in places, opening onto a turquoise reservoir where you rent a kayak or pedalo and paddle into the gorge mouth.
around:Gorges du Verdon & Lac de Sainte-.text: Europe's grandest limestone canyon, dropping to nearly 700 m in places, opening onto a turquoise reservoir where you rent a kayak or pedalo and paddle into the gorge mouth. The colour isn't filtered — the Verdon runs milky jade from fluorine, microalgae and fine mineral particles held in suspension. Go weekday and early. The lake basin is man-made, filled 1973–74; it drowned old Les Salles-sur-Verdon, whose last houses were dynamited in March 1974.

around:Moustiers-Sainte-Marie.name: Moustiers-Sainte-Marie
around:Moustiers-Sainte-Marie.label: ~2h north, at the Verdon's gate (just over the line in Alpes-de-Haute-Provence)
around:Moustiers-Sainte-Marie.hook: A Plus Beau Village wedged into a cliff cleft, famous for tin-glazed faïence since the 17th century, with a gilded star strung on a chain between two rock faces.
around:Moustiers-Sainte-Marie.text: A Plus Beau Village wedged into a cliff cleft, famous for tin-glazed faïence since the 17th century, with a gilded star strung on a chain between two rock faces. The star is the village's oldest legend — supposedly hung by a returning crusader as a votive offering. Pair it with the Verdon; the two are one outing. Faïence workshops still fire here.

around:Porquerolles & Port-Cros (Îles d'.name: Porquerolles & Port-Cros (Îles d'Or)
around:Porquerolles & Port-Cros (Îles d'.label: 15–35 min by boat from Giens / Hyères port
around:Porquerolles & Port-Cros (Îles d'.hook: Two of the Golden Islands: Porquerolles for white-sand coves, vineyards and the Fondation Carmignac art foundation; Port-Cros for wild trails and no cars.
around:Porquerolles & Port-Cros (Îles d'.text: Two of the Golden Islands: Porquerolles for white-sand coves, vineyards and the Fondation Carmignac art foundation; Port-Cros for wild trails and no cars. Port-Cros became France's (and Europe's) first marine national park in 1963 — snorkel its underwater trail. Porquerolles was a 1912 wedding gift from industrialist François Fournier to his wife; the state bought most of it in 1971, and its Conservatoire vineyards preserve heritage vines.

around:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des.name: Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des Méditerranées
around:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des.label: ~50 min east on the Corniche des Maures
around:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des.hook: A twenty-hectare seaside domain whose gardens landscape philosopher Gilles Clément replanted from 1989 with the floras of every Mediterranean-climate zone on earth — California, Chile, South Africa, South Australia — tumbling to a turquoise cove.
around:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des.text: A twenty-hectare seaside domain whose gardens landscape philosopher Gilles Clément replanted from 1989 with the floras of every Mediterranean-climate zone on earth — California, Chile, South Africa, South Australia — tumbling to a turquoise cove. Clément's 'garden in movement' made concrete: no clipped parterres, just curated wildness, managed ecologically. Owned by the Conservatoire du Littoral. The same coast road strings past Bormes-les-Mimosas and, further east, the hill villages of Gassin and Ramatuelle.

around:Massif des Maures — Collobrières.name: Massif des Maures — Collobrières & Chartreuse de la Verne
around:Massif des Maures — Collobrières.label: ~50 min–1h drive inland from Hyères
around:Massif des Maures — Collobrières.hook: A dark massif of cork oak and chestnut forest around Collobrières, the chestnut capital, with a Carthusian monastery, La Verne, hidden about 12 km deeper on a rough track.
around:Massif des Maures — Collobrières.text: A dark massif of cork oak and chestnut forest around Collobrières, the chestnut capital, with a Carthusian monastery, La Verne, hidden about 12 km deeper on a rough track. The Maures is geologically alien to Provence — ancient crystalline schist, not limestone, which is why chestnuts and cork oaks thrive. La Verne was founded by the Carthusians in 1170. Come for the Fête de la Châtaigne on three October Sundays (in 2026: the 11th, 18th and 25th); the marrons glacés are the real thing.

around:Cotignac.name: Cotignac
around:Cotignac.label: ~1h10 drive north
around:Cotignac.hook: A Plus Beau Village strung under an ~80-metre tuff cliff riddled with troglodyte dwellings and pigeonniers, ringed by vineyards and plane-shaded squares.
around:Cotignac.text: A Plus Beau Village strung under an ~80-metre tuff cliff riddled with troglodyte dwellings and pigeonniers, ringed by vineyards and plane-shaded squares. The soft tufa rock let villagers carve homes and refuges straight into the cliff — some still accessible. A working wine village, not a museum; it only earned the Plus Beaux Villages label in October 2022. Time it with the market.

around:Tourtour & Aups (Haut Var).name: Tourtour & Aups (Haut Var)
around:Tourtour & Aups (Haut Var).label: ~1h15–1h30 drive north
around:Tourtour & Aups (Haut Var).hook: Tourtour, a Plus Beau Village and 'village in the sky' at 635 m with long views over the Haut-Var; nearby Aups, the black-truffle capital.
around:Tourtour & Aups (Haut Var).text: Tourtour, a Plus Beau Village and 'village in the sky' at 635 m with long views over the Haut-Var; nearby Aups, the black-truffle capital. Aups holds one of Provence's great truffle markets every Thursday morning from November to February — Tuber melanosporum, cash only, checked under the nose. Off-season it's a quiet stone village; the truffle is the reason to time it right.

around:Bandol wine country — La Cadière-.name: Bandol wine country — La Cadière-d'Azur & Domaine Tempier
around:Bandol wine country — La Cadière-.label: ~35–45 min drive west of Toulon
around:Bandol wine country — La Cadière-.hook: Terraced Mourvèdre vineyards climbing between the hilltop villages of La Cadière-d'Azur and Le Castellet, home to Bandol's cult estate, Domaine Tempier.
around:Bandol wine country — La Cadière-.text: Terraced Mourvèdre vineyards climbing between the hilltop villages of La Cadière-d'Azur and Le Castellet, home to Bandol's cult estate, Domaine Tempier. Bandol reds are built on Mourvèdre, a late-ripening grape that only fully works in this sun-trap amphitheatre facing the sea. Tempier — run by the Peyraud family since 1940, whose Lucien is called the 'spiritual father' of Bandol — is the name that made the appellation serious and age-worthy; tastings by appointment, so call ahead.

drink:Bandol Rouge (Mourvèdre).name: Bandol Rouge (Mourvèdre)
drink:Bandol Rouge (Mourvèdre).hook: The one Var wine built to age like a serious red, because the appellation forces it to: at least 50% Mourvèdre, and eighteen months' ageing - much of it in old-oak foudre - before release. Late-ripening Mourvèdre only finishes fully in this sea-facing amphitheatre of limestone terraces (Pibarnon climbs to 300m), which is why no other French appellation is built around it. Young, it drinks of leather, garrigue and black olive more than fruit; decant it.

drink:Bandol Rosé.name: Bandol Rosé
drink:Bandol Rosé.hook: Not the pale poolside kind. Tempier's rosé runs roughly 55% Mourvèdre - darker and structured, built for bouillabaisse rather than sunbathing. It was Domaine Tempier, carried to America by importer Kermit Lynch from the late 1970s, that taught drinkers a Provençal rosé could be a serious wine. Treat it like a light red: it takes fish soup, aïoli, even lamb.

drink:Côtes de Provence Rosé.name: Côtes de Provence Rosé
drink:Côtes de Provence Rosé.hook: The everyday Var pour, and an industry: rosé is around 80% of the appellation's output, mostly Grenache-Cinsault-Syrah pressed pale and bone-dry. Drink the most recent vintage, cold and young - it is not built to keep, and last year's bottle is already tiring.

drink:Bellet (the Riviera neighbour).name: Bellet (the Riviera neighbour)
drink:Bellet (the Riviera neighbour).hook: Be honest - Bellet is not in the Var. It sits inside the city limits of Nice (Alpes-Maritimes), one of France's smallest AOCs at about 55 hectares, and it earns a place here because nothing else on the coast tastes like it. Whites are Rolle (Vermentino); reds and rosés lean on two near-endemic grapes, Braquet and Folle Noire (Fuella). Production is tiny and rarely leaves the region - a bottle to hunt, not to expect.

drink:Pastis.name: Pastis
drink:Pastis.hook: The 6pm ritual, not a wine. Star anise, liquorice and garrigue herbs, cut roughly five parts cold water to one until it louches milky - water first, then ice, so the anethole doesn't clump. It is not made in the Var: Ricard is Marseille's child, created there in 1932 amid the wave of pastis that filled the void left by the 1915 absinthe ban. Reach for Henri Bardouin, built on more than sixty plants and spices, if you want to taste the herbs past the liquorice.

drink:Fleur de Figue (fig liqueur).hook: The Var's other obsession is the fig - the violet Bourjassotte Noire of Solliès-Pont, France's only AOP fig. This liqueur, macerated and bottled in the Var at Taradeau, is September in a glass: a digestif, or splashed into cold rosé or sparkling wine as an apéritif. Real fruit, none of the synthetic fig-candy note.

drink:Liqueur de châtaigne / Crème de ma.hook: Collobrières, deep in the Massif des Maures, is the chestnut capital of the coast, its wooded slopes long planted with châtaigneraies. The Confiserie Azuréenne - making marrons glacés since 1945 - turns the chestnut into everything, alcohol included, alongside its celebrated crème de marrons. Autumn drinking; the village chestnut festival fills the last three Sundays of October.

landmarks:Villa Noailles (Hyères).name: Villa Noailles (Hyères)
landmarks:Villa Noailles (Hyères).hook: Robert Mallet-Stevens's modernist villa in the hills above Hyères, begun in 1923 for arts patrons Charles and Marie-Laure de Noailles - the house that drew Man Ray, Buñuel and Giacometti into their circle. Now an art centre for design, architecture, fashion and photography, and each October home to the Hyères International Festival of fashion and photography.

landmarks:Rade de Toulon (from Mont Faro.hook: One of Europe's great natural roadsteads and the home port of the French Mediterranean fleet, seen whole from the summit of Mont Faron (584m): the harbour, the naval base, the Massif de la Sainte-Baume beyond on a clear day. A memorial to the August 1944 Allied landings in Provence sits at the top.

landmarks:Fort de Brégançon.name: Fort de Brégançon
landmarks:Fort de Brégançon.hook: An island fortress on a rocky islet off Bormes-les-Mimosas, fortified over the centuries, that has been the French President's holiday residence since 1968. Opened to guided visits in 2014.
landmarks:Fort de Brégançon.text: An island fortress on a rocky islet off Bormes-les-Mimosas, fortified over the centuries, that has been the French President's holiday residence since 1968. Opened to guided visits in 2014. Signal Guided tour only, about three hours on foot, booked ahead through the Bormes-les-Mimosas tourist office (no tickets on site); adult €12 (reduced €10). Limited dates in season, groups capped at 20, steep and not suited to reduced mobility - and it closes for presidential use, so confirm it is actually running.

landmarks:Chartreuse de la Verne.name: Chartreuse de la Verne
landmarks:Chartreuse de la Verne.hook: A Carthusian monastery founded around 1170, isolated deep in the Massif des Maures and built largely from the local greenish serpentine stone. Listed as a historic monument since 1921; today home to the contemplative Sisters of Bethlehem.
landmarks:Chartreuse de la Verne.text: A Carthusian monastery founded around 1170, isolated deep in the Massif des Maures and built largely from the local greenish serpentine stone. Listed as a historic monument since 1921; today home to the contemplative Sisters of Bethlehem. Signal Open most of the year, self-guided with a booklet: 11am-6pm June-August, 11am-5pm the rest of the season; closed in January and on religious holidays; adult €7. From about 21 June to 20 September the forest road (RD214) up to it can shut for fire risk - check with the Collobrières tourist office before driving. Silence is requested; dress modestly.

landmarks:Citadelle de Saint-Tropez.name: Citadelle de Saint-Tropez
landmarks:Citadelle de Saint-Tropez.hook: The hexagonal hilltop keep above the port, built 1602-08, now the Musée d'histoire maritime telling St-Tropez's sea story from the Bailli de Suffren to the sardine fleet. The finest panorama over the gulf and the Maures.
landmarks:Citadelle de Saint-Tropez.text: The hexagonal hilltop keep above the port, built 1602-08, now the Musée d'histoire maritime telling St-Tropez's sea story from the Bailli de Suffren to the sardine fleet. The finest panorama over the gulf and the Maures. Signal Open daily 10am-6.30pm (Apr-Sep), 10am-5.30pm (Oct-Mar); adult a few euros. Climb up through the old town; the ramparts and the view reward the walk as much as the museum.

landmarks:Église Notre-Dame-de-l'Assompt.name: Église Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption (Saint-Tropez)
landmarks:Église Notre-Dame-de-l'Assompt.hook: The Italian-baroque parish church whose ochre-and-sienna bell tower is the town's emblem on every postcard. Inside sits the gilded bust of Saint Torpes, carried through the streets each May during the Bravade.
landmarks:Église Notre-Dame-de-l'Assompt.text: The Italian-baroque parish church whose ochre-and-sienna bell tower is the town's emblem on every postcard. Signal Free, open in daytime outside services, in the old town just below the citadelle (coordinates approximate). Come mid-May (16-18 May) for the Bravade if you want the church alive rather than a quiet photo stop.

culture:Villa Noailles.name: Villa Noailles
culture:Villa Noailles.hook: Robert Mallet-Stevens' 1920s modernist villa above Hyères, now an art centre, with a triangular Cubist garden and two summer festivals born inside it.
culture:Villa Noailles.text: Robert Mallet-Stevens' 1920s modernist villa above Hyères, now an art centre, with a triangular Cubist garden and two summer festivals born inside it. Charles and Marie-Laure de Noailles, the most reckless art patrons of their day, handed the young Robert Mallet-Stevens a hillside and asked for 'an interesting little house to live in.' In successive campaigns from 1923 to 1933 he answered with a white, cubic manifesto of the Modern Movement: indoor pool, gymnasium, squash court, and a triangular Cubist garden built in 1926-27 by Gabriel Guévrékian, once crowned by Jacques Lipchitz's bronze 'La Joie de Vivre,' which rotated on its base every four minutes. The couple bankrolled the avant-garde with the same open hand: Buñuel's scandalous L'Age d'Or and Man Ray's 'Les Mystères du Château du Dé' (shot here in 1929) were their money. Hyères took the house over in 1973; today it hosts the two events it spawned, the Hyères International Festival of Fashion & Photography (founded 1985 by Jean-Pierre Blanc, then 21, and now the oldest young-designer fashion competition in the world) and Design Parade. The one real thing to carry away: this is where modernism learned it was allowed to be joyful, not just severe. Signal Built in campaigns 1923-1933 by Robert Mallet-Stevens; municipal art centre since 1973; Design Parade held 25-28 June 2026

culture:Fondation Carmignac (Villa Carmi.name: Fondation Carmignac (Villa Carmignac)
culture:Fondation Carmignac (Villa Carmi.hook: A contemporary-art foundation buried under a restored Provençal farmhouse on a car-free national-park island, walked barefoot.
culture:Fondation Carmignac (Villa Carmi.text: A contemporary-art foundation buried under a restored Provençal farmhouse on a car-free national-park island, walked barefoot. Financier and collector Édouard Carmignac sank a 2,000 m² gallery beneath an old mas and a ceiling of water on the protected island of Porquerolles, opening it in 2018. You leave your shoes at the door and cross the galleries barefoot before spilling into a fifteen-hectare garden studded with sculpture. Because Porquerolles is a national park, you arrive only by boat and there are no cars, so the art is framed by umbrella pines, salt air and heat-shimmer instead of white walls. Verified: the 2026 show 'Sea, Pop & Sun' (curated by Dieter Buchhart and Anna Karina Hofbauer, setting Warhol, Lichtenstein and Martial Raysse against living artists) runs 25 April to 1 November. The real thing to know: it borrows its title from a summer mood and is engineered to feel like a daydream rather than a museum. Signal Opened 2018 by Édouard Carmignac; 2026 exhibition 25 Apr-1 Nov

culture:Domaine Tempier.name: Domaine Tempier
culture:Domaine Tempier.hook: The estate that made Bandol serious wine, and whose rosé is one of the Mediterranean's genuinely beautiful drinks.
culture:Domaine Tempier.text: The estate that made Bandol serious wine, and whose rosé is one of the Mediterranean's genuinely beautiful drinks. This is the terroir story of the Var itself. The Tempier family had held the domaine since 1834; in 1936 Lucie Tempier married Lucien Peyraud and her father gave the couple the estate, which they took over around 1940. Together they fought to win Bandol its own appellation (granted 11 November 1941) and, on 27 October 1943, bottled the estate's first wine, a rosé, instead of selling in bulk. Bandol is mourvèdre country, sun-baked, saline, structured, and Tempier proved it could age for decades. Lucie 'Lulu' Peyraud (1917-2020) was also a self-taught cook whose long feasts became legend; the American writer Richard Olney gave her a whole book, 'Lulu's Provençal Table' (1994), and her disciples Alice Waters of Chez Panisse and importer Kermit Lynch carried her name across the world. The real thing: the pale, mineral Bandol rosé you drink up and down this coast exists in its modern form largely because of one family in the hills above Bandol. Signal Estate in the Tempier family since 1834; Peyrauds drove Bandol AOC (1941); first bottled wine (rosé) 1943; Lulu Peyraud 1917-2020

culture:La Tarte Tropézienne (Alexandre.name: La Tarte Tropézienne (Alexandre Micka)
culture:La Tarte Tropézienne (Alexandre.hook: The cream-filled brioche invented and still sold here, the pastry Bardot named.
culture:La Tarte Tropézienne (Alexandre.text: The cream-filled brioche invented and still sold here, the pastry Bardot named. In 1945 a Polish confectioner named Alexandre Micka settled in Saint-Tropez, bringing a family recipe for a sugar-crusted brioche split and filled with two creams. In 1955, catering the shoot of 'And God Created Woman,' he served it to Brigitte Bardot, who suggested he call it 'la tarte de Saint-Tropez'; Micka kept the idea and trademarked the name Tarte Tropézienne in 1973. His original shop still trades under that name. Not a drink, but the definitive edible souvenir of the peninsula and the perfect foil to a glass of cold rosé. The real thing: the town's most famous dessert was christened by an accident of cinema, and the woman who named it never took a centime for it. Signal Micka settled 1945; tarte created 1955; named by Brigitte Bardot; trademarked 1973; original shop still open

hotel-bars:Les Caves du Roy — Hôtel Bybl.name: Les Caves du Roy — Hôtel Byblos
hotel-bars:Les Caves du Roy — Hôtel Bybl.hook: The legendary cellar nightclub-bar inside the Byblos, open only in season.
hotel-bars:Les Caves du Roy — Hôtel Bybl.text: The legendary cellar nightclub-bar inside the Byblos, open only in season. The whole hotel is a love letter to a muse: Lebanese businessman Jean-Prosper Gay-Para built the Byblos as a 'palace of a thousand and one nights' inspired by Brigitte Bardot, a faux-Provençal hamlet in apricot and salmon stucco inaugurated on 27 May 1967 with godmothers Bardot and Mireille Darc and three days of festivities for more than 700 guests. Its cellar-bar, Les Caves du Roy, has been the 'temple of Tropezian nights' since July 1967, with Juliette Gréco, Françoise Sagan and Jacques Chazot at the opening and Mick and Bianca Jagger's wedding celebrated here in 1971. Gay-Para lost the hotel within months, selling to Sylvain Floirat on 19 September 1967 after the Six-Day War pulled him back to Beirut; the Floirat family has kept the flame for over fifty years. The real thing: the legend is deliberately rationed, weekends only in spring and autumn and nightly only across high summer, roughly late June to end of August. Signal Byblos inaugurated 27 May 1967; Caves du Roy open since July 1967; seasonal, nightly late Jun-late Aug (2026)

hotel-bars:Bar de La Ponche.name: Bar de La Ponche
hotel-bars:Bar de La Ponche.hook: The bar of a discreet 5-star hotel in the old fishermen's quarter where the Tropezian myth actually began.
hotel-bars:Bar de La Ponche.text: The bar of a discreet 5-star hotel in the old fishermen's quarter where the Tropezian myth actually began. Before Saint-Tropez was Saint-Tropez, La Ponche was a fishermen's inn in the eponymous old quarter, run for generations by the Duckstein family. In 1949 Boris Vian annexed the neighbouring barn to make a bar, and through the 1950s it filled with the New Wave: Bardot's laughter, Vian's trumpet, Vadim shooting scenes for 'And God Created Woman' a few metres down the lane, Sagan, Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir drifting through. Reopened as a year-round five-star in 2021 after an eight-month renovation redesigned by Fabrizio Casiraghi, it kept its low-key soul. The real thing: this shadowed corner above the little port, not the superyacht quay, is where the whole Tropezian legend was actually lit. Signal Bar created 1949 by Boris Vian; reopened year-round 5-star 2021, redesign by Fabrizio Casiraghi

hotel-bars:Terrasse de la Villa Belrose.name: Terrasse de la Villa Belrose
hotel-bars:Terrasse de la Villa Belrose.hook: A panoramic terrace bar high in the Gassin hills for a glass of rosé over the whole bay.
hotel-bars:Terrasse de la Villa Belrose.text: A panoramic terrace bar high in the Gassin hills for a glass of rosé over the whole bay. The genius of the Althoff Villa Belrose is altitude and distance: it sits five minutes but a whole world away from the Saint-Tropez crush, on a Gassin hillside where the terrace hangs above the roadstead and the pool. You come here not for a scene but for the oldest ritual on this coast, a cold glass of Provence rosé while the light goes long over the gulf and the yachts below shrink to toys. The gastronomy carries a real name, chef Jimmy Coutel's 'Le Belrose' (Coutel has led the kitchen since 2022), but the terrace apéritif is the point. The real thing: this is a Leading Hotel of the World that trades entirely on the view, and it closes for winter, so the drink is a summer-season pleasure. Signal Leading Hotels of the World; reopened 24 April 2026 for the season, closes for winter; chef Jimmy Coutel since 2022

hotel-bars:Bar du Sube.name: Bar du Sube
hotel-bars:Bar du Sube.hook: A first-floor balcony bar with the oldest terrace in town, looking straight down the working port.
hotel-bars:Bar du Sube.text: A first-floor balcony bar with the oldest terrace in town, looking straight down the working port. The Sube is the anti-Byblos: a modest, centuries-old three-star hotel right on the quay whose first-floor balcony is said to be the oldest in Saint-Tropez, and whose bar is a front-row seat on the endless choreography of yachts and sailing boats coming and going. Its five small terrace tables are the most fought-over in town. Climb higher and there is an English bar of mahogany and model boats, with a fireplace, subdued light and Art Deco panelling, a sailors' snug that nods to the town's 'Les Voiles' regatta rather than any nightclub. The real thing: for the price of one drink you get the single best free theatre on the port, from a perch that predates every palace on the peninsula. Signal Historic 3-star port hotel; oldest balcony in town over the harbour; mahogany English/Art Deco bar above

hotel-bars:Bar Le Soleil d'Eau — Château.name: Bar Le Soleil d'Eau — Château de la Messardière
hotel-bars:Bar Le Soleil d'Eau — Château.hook: A terrace aperitif at a fairy-tale hilltop château-palace above the town.
hotel-bars:Bar Le Soleil d'Eau — Château.text: A terrace aperitif at a fairy-tale hilltop château-palace above the town. The Messardière is a 19th-century folly with turrets, domes and arcades, built as a wedding gift from cognac merchant Gabriel Dupuy d'Angeac to his daughter Louise and her husband, cavalry officer Henry Brisson de La Messardière, and perched in a 25-acre park of umbrella pines and cypress above Saint-Tropez. It joined the Airelles collection in 2019 and reopened as a palace in July 2021; the drink to take is on the terrace of the Bar Le Soleil d'Eau, aperitif in hand, with the Gulf of Saint-Tropez laid out below and the pine-resin heat all around. The real thing: this is the largest hotel in Saint-Tropez, yet its pleasure is the oldest and simplest, height, shade, and a slow glass while the bay turns gold. Signal 19th-century château (wedding gift, Dupuy d'Angeac family); Airelles Collection since 2019, reopened as palace July 2021

hotel-bars:Sénéquier.name: Sénéquier
hotel-bars:Sénéquier.hook: The red-chaired café on the quay, an open-air observatory of the port since the age of the New Wave.
hotel-bars:Sénéquier.text: The red-chaired café on the quay, an open-air observatory of the port since the age of the New Wave. Sénéquier began as a patisserie founded in 1887 by Marie and Martin Sénéquier, pastry-makers already famous for a white nougat of Spanish almonds, Sicilian pistachios and Provence honey. In 1930 Lisette Sénéquier turned it into a café and tea room on the harbour, and its unmistakable bright-red tables and chairs became the front row for the Nouvelle Vague and everyone after. Bombed in 1944 and rebuilt by 1951, its thirty-metre terrace of director's chairs and triangular tables is still the most conspicuous seat on the quay. The real thing: order a drink here and you are paying for a sightline, not the glass, it is the most famous café on the Riviera precisely because it faces the whole promenade of the port. Signal Patisserie founded 1887 (Marie & Martin Sénéquier); harbour café from 1930; rebuilt 1951; landmark red terrace

walks:Sentier Blanc-Martel.name: Sentier Blanc-Martel
walks:Sentier Blanc-Martel.hook: The Verdon's flagship hike: a roughly 16 km one-way descent into Europe's deepest river canyon, with steel ladders and a long unlit tunnel of around 670 m (bring a torch), from La Maline down to the Couloir Samson. A navette shuttle links the two trailheads so you don't double back.
walks:Sentier Blanc-Martel.text: The Verdon's flagship hike: a roughly 16 km one-way descent into Europe's deepest river canyon, with steel ladders and a long unlit tunnel of around 670 m (bring a torch), from La Maline down to the Couloir Samson. A navette shuttle links the two trailheads so you don't double back. Named for the two men behind the first full traverse of the canyon in August 1905: Paris speleologist Edouard-Alfred Martel, sent by the Ministry of Agriculture to survey drinking water for Provence (the Fontaine-l'Eveque spring), and Isidore Blanc, the naturalist schoolmaster of Rougon who guided him. The Touring Club de France engineered the trail proper, ladders at the Breche Imbert and all, between 1926 and 1928; Blanc, made a TCF delegate, worked it up until his accidental death in 1933, and the path was renamed Blanc-Martel in his honour in 2005. Honesty by negation: the path itself runs on the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence bank, not the Var; the Var owns the south rim (the Corniche Sublime belvederes above Aiguines). The wilder Imbut/Styx trail on the Var bank has been closed by municipal order since July 2022 for rockfall, so this is the canyon walk that is actually open. Signal First full canyon traverse by Martel and Blanc, August 1905; trail engineered by the Touring Club de France 1926-1928; renamed Blanc-Martel in 2005.

walks:Presqu'ile de Giens, double tombol.name: Presqu'ile de Giens, double tombolo & Salins des Pesquiers
walks:Presqu'ile de Giens, double tombol.hook: A peninsula lashed to the coast by two parallel sand bars, one of only a handful of double tombolos on Earth (three to five worldwide), enclosing old salt pans; the sentier du littoral rounds the wild, wind-hammered west and south shores.
walks:Presqu'ile de Giens, double tombol.text: A peninsula lashed to the coast by two parallel sand bars, one of only a handful of double tombolos on Earth (three to five worldwide), enclosing old salt pans; the sentier du littoral rounds the wild, wind-hammered west and south shores. The salt works, run by the Compagnie des Salins du Midi, closed in 1995; the Conservatoire du littoral now owns the marsh (since 2001), a roost for pink flamingos year-round that peaks around 2,000 birds in late summer. The coast path you walk is the old sentier des douaniers, the early-19th-century customs path along which patrols once watched the shore for contraband, and it is the very right-of-way that a 1976 French law fixed nationwide as a public easement (a 3 m passage across private coastal land), later reinforced by the 1986 loi Littoral. Signal Salt production ceased 1995; marsh Conservatoire-owned since 2001, flamingos year-round; path is the old sentier des douaniers, and the 3 m coastal easement was set by a 1976 law (loi Littoral 1986).

walks:Collobrieres.name: Collobrieres
walks:Collobrieres.hook: A stone village on a chestnut-shaded river deep inside the Maures, ringed by roughly 2,000 hectares of chestnut groves; the trailhead for the best Maures walks (up to La Verne, up to Notre-Dame-des-Anges) and the self-declared capital of the chestnut.
walks:Collobrieres.text: A stone village on a chestnut-shaded river deep inside the Maures, ringed by roughly 2,000 hectares of chestnut groves; the trailhead for the best Maures walks (up to La Verne, up to Notre-Dame-des-Anges) and the self-declared capital of the chestnut. The sweet chestnut is the Maures' terroir tree, and the Confiserie Azureenne has candied its marrons in the village for over half a century, roughly seven days steeping in vanilla-scented syrup to make a single marron glace, while the village throws its chestnut festival across three Sundays each October. One real thing to carry away: the marron is a selected large-fruited variety of the wild chataigne, not a separate nut. Signal Chestnut festival held three Sundays each October; Confiserie Azureenne candying marrons here 50-plus years.

calas:Plage Notre-Dame, Porquerolles.name: Plage Notre-Dame, Porquerolles
calas:Plage Notre-Dame, Porquerolles.hook: 800 m of pale sand backed by Aleppo pines that run almost to the water, a 30-min walk or bike from the car-free village, and angled so it shelters from both the Mistral and the east wind.
calas:Plage Notre-Dame, Porquerolles.text: 800 m of pale sand backed by Aleppo pines that run almost to the water, a 30-min walk or bike from the car-free village, and angled so it shelters from both the Mistral and the east wind. The whole island was a wedding gift. On 22 February 1912 Francois-Joseph Fournier, a Belgian boatman's son who made a gold fortune on the Veta Verde lode in Mexico, bought nearly all of the island's 1,254 hectares at auction for his wife Sylvia, then planted the eucalyptus, mimosa and umbrella pines that still shade the paths. European Best Destinations voted Notre-Dame the most beautiful beach in Europe in 2015, and it has paid for the fame: a 6,000-visitor daily summer cap (in place since 2021) and compulsory ferry booking now guard the freshwater table and the island's rich flora. Signal Island bought 22 Feb 1912 by Fournier; named Europe's most beautiful beach 2015; 6,000/day summer quota since 2021.

calas:Cap Taillat.name: Cap Taillat
calas:Cap Taillat.hook: A wild sand isthmus tying a scrub islet to the mainland, reached on 2.5 km of coastal path through maquis, with a Neolithic dolmen (the Dolmen de Briande, excavated 1935, the southernmost in the Var) on the ridge above and swimmable coves on either flank of the tombolo.
calas:Cap Taillat.text: A wild sand isthmus tying a scrub islet to the mainland, reached on 2.5 km of coastal path through maquis, with a Neolithic dolmen (the Dolmen de Briande, excavated 1935, the southernmost in the Var) on the ridge above and swimmable coves on either flank of the tombolo. It is wilderness today only because a Club Med was stopped here: a company bought 27 hectares in 1970 to build 400 bungalows and a marina, Ramatuelle's mayor called in the Conservatoire du littoral, and it bought Cap Taillat in 1987. A fire on 24 July 2017 burned some 550 hectares across Taillat and neighbouring Cap Lardier to ash; the cistus and heather maquis has been regrowing since, which is why the vegetation looks so young. Signal 27 ha bought for a 400-bungalow Club Med in 1970; saved by the Conservatoire du littoral (Cap Taillat acquired 1987); 24 July 2017 fire burned ~550 ha.

secret-gems:Sentier sous-marin de la Pal.name: Sentier sous-marin de la Palud, Port-Cros
secret-gems:Sentier sous-marin de la Pal.hook: A 40-45 min walk from the harbour to the Plage de la Palud, then a free, marked snorkel loop (mask, fins, tuba) past six submerged interpretation buoys in a few metres of water, among grouper, wrasse and posidonia meadow.
secret-gems:Sentier sous-marin de la Pal.text: A 40-45 min walk from the harbour to the Plage de la Palud, then a free, marked snorkel loop (mask, fins, tuba) past six submerged interpretation buoys in a few metres of water, among grouper, wrasse and posidonia meadow. Port-Cros became the first marine national park in Europe by decree of 14 December 1963, born of a donation rather than a purchase: the Henrys had run the island since 1921, and Marceline Henry gave a third of it (213 hectares of the western island) to the State on condition it be protected, with Andre Malraux carrying it through. The underwater trail here, laid in 1979, was the first in France. The real lesson: on this island you read the sea on foot, not just the land, and the fish are unafraid because nobody has speared them in over 60 years. Signal National park by decree of 14 Dec 1963 (first marine park in Europe); underwater trail opened 1979 (first in France).

secret-gems:Chartreuse de la Verne.name: Chartreuse de la Verne
secret-gems:Chartreuse de la Verne.hook: A huge, near-black monastery built of green Maures serpentine, hidden on a forested ridge above the chestnut woods and reached only by a rough road; a working silent cloister with a partial visitor route.
secret-gems:Chartreuse de la Verne.text: A huge, near-black monastery built of green Maures serpentine, hidden on a forested ridge above the chestnut woods and reached only by a rough road; a working silent cloister with a partial visitor route. Founded around 1170 by the bishops of Toulon (Pierre Isnard) and Frejus (Fredol d'Anduze); the first Romanesque church was consecrated on 3 October 1174, pillaged by the lords of Bormes in 1416, and emptied when the Carthusians left for Italy at the Revolution (its property confiscated by decree of 2 November 1789). The green serpentine framing its portals was quarried nearby in the Maures and hauled up by mule, the local stone made monumental. Silent again since 1983, when the monastic Family of Bethlehem moved in. Honesty: much is enclosed, so you visit the edges of a living silence, not a museum. Signal Founded c.1170, church consecrated 1174, pillaged by the lords of Bormes 1416; monastic Family of Bethlehem in residence since 1983.

secret-gems:Village des Tortues, Carnoul.name: Village des Tortues, Carnoules
secret-gems:Village des Tortues, Carnoul.hook: A 2-hectare sanctuary and veterinary clinic at the foot of the massif where you walk among Hermann's tortoises: rescue, breeding pens, incubation and a release programme.
secret-gems:Village des Tortues, Carnoul.text: A 2-hectare sanctuary and veterinary clinic at the foot of the massif where you walk among Hermann's tortoises: rescue, breeding pens, incubation and a release programme. The Maures and the neighbouring Plaine des Maures hold the last wild population of Hermann's tortoise on the French mainland. Naturalists Bernard Devaux and David Stubbs founded the SOPTOM association in 1986 and opened the first village at Gonfaron on 28 May 1988; it moved to its current Carnoules site in June 2017. The one real thing it teaches: France's only native land tortoise survives essentially here, and its two great killers are summer wildfire and the roads that cut its range. Signal SOPTOM founded 1986; village opened 28 May 1988 (Gonfaron); relocated to Carnoules June 2017.

secret-gems:Domaine du Rayol, Le Jardin.name: Domaine du Rayol, Le Jardin des Mediterranees
secret-gems:Domaine du Rayol, Le Jardin.hook: 20 hectares of protected coast (7 of garden, 13 of maquis) facing the Port-Cros islands, with a grand antique-style pergola and cypress-lined stair down to the sea and, in summer, a guided snorkel trail in the bay.
secret-gems:Domaine du Rayol, Le Jardin.text: 20 hectares of protected coast (7 of garden, 13 of maquis) facing the Port-Cros islands, with a grand antique-style pergola and cypress-lined stair down to the sea and, in summer, a guided snorkel trail in the bay. The Conservatoire du littoral rescued the abandoned estate in 1989 and handed it to landscape gardener Gilles Clement, who refused a manicured garden and instead planted a mosaic of the world's other Mediterranean climates: South African fynbos, Chilean matorral, Californian chaparral, Australian kwongan and mallee, all thriving under the same Var sun. The monumental pergola was raised around 1910 for the estate's first owner, the Parisian businessman Alfred Courmes; the aviator Henri Potez, who bought the domain in 1940, later drove the long cypress-lined stair down through it. Terroir made literal, and gardened without irrigation or pesticides from the start. Signal Pergola built c.1910 for Alfred Courmes; estate bought by the Conservatoire du littoral 1989; garden conceived by Gilles Clement.
